div.p: The benefits of the limited preemption scheduling model serve to minimize preemption overhead while enabling cooperative scheduling between real-time tasks. Preemption point placement (PPP) algorithms are employed to select a suitable subset of preemption locations for limited preemption scheduling that optimize task worst case execution time. Similarly, preemption threshold scheduling enhances schedulability in a fully-preemptive environment by taking advantage of execution time slack in a task set by adjusting preemption thresholds to permit tasks to completely execute non-preemptively where possible. The ability to execute non-preemptively offers reduced cache related preemption delay (CRPD) further enhancing limited preemption schedulability.

In this work, we integrate limited preemption scheduling using preemption placement with preemption threshold scheduling to realize further task set schedulability benefits. A case study using synthetically generated tasksets will demonstrate the significantly improved (up to a 30% increase in breakdown utilization) schedulability benefits of our proposed integrated PPP and optimal threshold assignment (OTA) algorithm.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The utility of real-time system computations depends on two important properties, correctness and timeliness. The timeliness property (the subject of schedulability analysis) is concerned with ensuring real-time task computations are completed within required deadlines. Designers of real-time systems must choose the scheduling paradigm that will ultimately determine if the real-time task set will meet its timeliness objectives. The available choices are 1) nonpreemptive scheduling, 2) fully-preemptive scheduling, and 3) limited preemption scheduling. Non-preemptive scheduling suffers from blocking of high priority tasks and fully preemptive scheduling suffers from substantial preemption overhead (up to 44% [1]- [3] of a tasks worst case execution time (WCET)) each approach degrading task set schedulability. Limited preemption scheduling attempts to 1) reduce blocking by limiting the number of allowed preemptions, maximizing non-preemptive task execution and 2) reduce preemption overhead via non-preemptive regions. Regardless of the chosen scheduling paradigm, effective schedulability analysis of real-time task sets mandates accurate WCET and cache related preemption delay (CRPD) estimates. The recognized benefits of limited preemption scheduling [4] [5] have motivated recent work on preemption point placement (PPP) algorithms [6] [7]. In a complimentary fashion, preemption threshold scheduling [8] assigns preemption thresholds allowing tasks to execute non-preemptively where feasible. The two methods take advantage of inherent task set execution slack to enhance schedulability. The primary difference arises in the non-preemptive granularity. Limited preemption scheduling divides each task into non-preemptive chunks whereas preemption threshold scheduling (PTS) facilitates non-preemptive execution at the task level.

The importance of CRPD in schedulability analysis stems from it comprising the majority of preemption overhead. CRPD occurs when a task denoted τ i is preempted by one or more higher priority tasks denoted τ k . The execution of high priority tasks results in the eviction of cache memory blocks that must be subsequently reloaded when task τ i resumes execution. Two primary models of CRPD computation exist: 1) the independent CRPD cost model [9] [10] [11] [12] [13] [14] [15] [16] [17], and 2) the interdependent CRPD cost model [18]. The vast majority of CRPD research falls under the independent CRPD model. Here, costs are solely a function of the preemption location under consideration. Since the next preemption may occur at any forward point in the task code, independent CRPD methods must conservatively utilize the next code location corresponding to the maximum CRPD cost. The interdependent CRPD cost model, however, overcomes this limitation by considering and computing costs between each pair of task code locations thereby achieving more accuracy. A key factor in scheduling decisions, CRPD cost accuracy is of paramount importance to preemption placement, optimal threshold assignment, and schedulability algorithms.

PPP algorithms select preemption points for each task to 1) minimize the overall task WCET, and 2) ensure the execution time between adjacent preemptions is limited by the maximum non-preemptive region execution time. The maximum non-preemptive region execution time, denoted Q i , is determined via task set schedulability analysis. The motivation behind our work is that the potential benefits of preemption threshold scheduling can be integrated with existing PPP algorithms to further enhance task set schedulability. We observe two opportunities:

1) The effectiveness of PTS is limited by employing pessimistic independent CRPD methods. 2) Each task in PPP algorithms are subjected to CRPD from the set of higher priority tasks which can be subsequently reduced via non-preemptive task execution per optimal threshold assignment. The paper contributions are as follows:

1) New integrated PPP/PTS schedulability constraints in Section VI. 2) A new pseudo-polynomial integrated PPP/PTS algorithm that carefully sequences preemption placement with provably optimal threshold assignment to achieve optimal schedulability in Section VIII. 3) A comprehensive evaluation across a diverse set of synthetically generated real-time tasks demonstrating the schedulability benefits of our approach in Section IX. It is important to note that the integration of PPP with PTS is not straightforward. Fundamentally, the choice of preemption points and preemption thresholds are entirely dependent upon each other making it non-trivial to derive the optimal solution to both independently. Therefore, an integrated, more holistic optimization is required and that is what our paper proposes. In summary, our approach effectively integrates limited preemption scheduling via preemption placement with preemption threshold scheduling via optimal preemption threshold assignment resulting in improved schedulability.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. First, current limited preemption scheduling research efforts and related work is discussed in Section II. Section III describes our realtime task model terminology. The real-time conditional flow graph model is detailed in Section IV. Section V presents a formal statement describing the objective function for selecting preemptions in linear and conditional flowgraphs. Fixed priority (FP) limited preemption and FP preemption threshold schedulability analysis is reviewed in Section VI. Response time analysis of FP limited preemption and FP preemption threshold scheduling is derived in Section VII. Section VIII discusses our proposed algorithm that integrates preemption point placement and optimal preemption threshold assignment. A case study using synthetically generated task sets demonstrates improved schedulability in Section IX. Finally, Section X offers relevant conclusions along with proposed future work.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: Our integrated conditional PPP and preemption threshold algorithm leverages elements from one prominent area of real-time theory, limited preemption scheduling. We now briefly summarize the prior work in this area and describe how it relates to our proposed algorithm.

Research in limited preemption scheduling attempts to address well-known limitations of the non-preemptive and fully preemptive scheduling paradigms. Two limited preemption scheduling models are the deferred preemption scheduling model and the preemption threshold scheduling model.

First, the fixed preemption point model [4] and the floating point preemption model [5] are two distinct sub-categories of deferred preemption scheduling. In the floating preemption point model [5], the currently executing task continues executing for a maximum of Q i time units or runs to completion if the remaining execution time is less than Q i . The parameter Q i is computed via task set schedulability analysis [5] representing the maximum amount of blocking time that task τ i may impose on higher priority tasks. Since the start of the non-preemptive execution region coincides with the arrival of a higher priority task, region locations are nondeterministic or floating. In contrast, the fixed point preemption model [4] differs from the floating preemption point model in that the task code preemptions are confined to pre-defined time intervals that are computed offline. 1Second, preemption threshold scheduling [19] employs a modified priority based scheme to determine when tasks may be preempted. Each task in the preemption threshold scheduling [19] approach is assigned two distinct priority values, each for a different purpose. These priorities are known as the nominal static priority π i and a preemption threshold θ i priority. The preempting task τ k may only preempt the currently executing task τ i if τ k has a nominal priority π k exceeding the assigned preemption threshold θ i .

Fixed PPP algorithms sought to minimize preemption overhead in fixed priority task sets in early work by Simonson and Patel [20] and Lee et al. [9]. For tasks executing via preemption triggered floating non-preemptive regions, Marinho et al. [21] successfully computed an upper-bound on task CRPD. Lastly, work in fixed priority (FP) preemption threshold schedulability (PTS) analysis by Bril et al. [8], supporting task sets with arbitrary deadlines, successfully assigned optimal priority thresholds by minimizing independent CRPD costs, and later complimented with a simulated annealing algorithm optimizing task layout [22]. A limited preemption scheme with varying preemption thresholds (FPVS) for preemption points was proposed and shown to be superior to PTS [23]. The effectiveness of these heuristic solutions is limited by the employed cost model.

Bertogna et al. [6] [7] realized an optimal PPP algorithm with linear time complexity for strictly linear CFG structures. A pseudo-polynomial preemption point placement algorithm was realized by Peng et al. [24] supporting well structured series/parallel conditional CFG structures. The limitations of these solutions stem from utilizing the less accurate independent CRPD cost model as compared to the interdependent cost model accounting for the dependency between selected preemption points. Recently, a quadratic PPP algorithm was proposed by Cavicchio et al. [18] using the interdependent CRPD cost model for linear CFG structures.

In this paper, we integrate preemption threshold scheduling with limited preemption scheduling resulting in substantial improvements over previous PPP and PTS methods. We take advantage of available taskset execution slack to further reduce CRPD cost, recognizing the interplay between the non-preemptive execution that PTS offers and the fine grained interdependent CRPD model used in preemption placement. The benefits of our approach will be illustrated in a case study employing synthetically generated real-time tasks that will demonstrate substantial schedulability benefits (up to a 30% increase in breakdown utilization).

div.head: III. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: Our system contains a task set τ of n periodic or sporadic non self-suspending tasks (τ 1 , τ 2 , ..., τ j , ..., τ n ) each scheduled on a single uniprocessor. Tasks are assumed to be indexed in descending fixed-priority order. Each task τ i is characterized by a tuple (G i , C N P i , D i , T i ) where G i is a series/parallel graph describing the real-time task code, C N P i is the non-preemptive worst case execution time, D i is the relative deadline, and T i is the inter-arrival time or period. Each task τ i creates an infinite number of jobs, with the first job arriving at any time after system start time and subsequent jobs arriving no earlier than T i time units with an arbitrary deadline D i . The system utilizes a fixed-priority preemptive scheduler with each task/job containing N i + 1 basic blocks denoted (δ 0 i , δ 1 i , δ 2 i , ..., δ Ni i ). We introduce the basic block notation δ j i where i is the task identifier and j is the basic block identifier. A dummy basic block δ 0 i with zero WCET is added at the beginning of each task to capture the preemption that occurs prior to task execution. In our model, a basic block is a set of one or more instructions that execute non-preemptively. Basic blocks are essentially the vertices V i of a conditional control flow graph (CFG) connected by directed edges E i representing the execution sequence of one or more job instructions. Figure 1 shown below illustrates the conditional basic block connection structure with loops. The CFG for task

While several CRPD methods exist, any method may be used that is compatible with preemption placement algorithms. Preemption placement algorithms require a finer level of CRPD granularity where the preemption cost is known at each basic block location or between pairs of adjacent preemption points.

div.head: IV. REAL-TIME CONDITIONAL FLOW GRAPH
div.p: The types of real-time linear and conditional flow graphs used in our work belong to the class of graphs known as series-parallel flow graphs [30]. We use the series/parallel terminology to describe the supported CFGs. An example series-parallel graph is shown in Figure 1. To demonstrate the applicability of series-parallel graphs to modern realtime applications, well known and commonly used realtime structured programming language constructs such as ordered linear statement sequences, if-then statements, ifthen-else statements, switch statements, bounded unrolled loops, and inline functions [31] comprise the supported software artifacts. One can readily observe that series-parallel graphs are partitioned into series and parallel connected linear code sections of basic blocks each having single entry and exit points. Due to the constrained resources of most real-time embedded processors, well written programs must employ a safe subset of programming language constructs such as conditional statements, bounded loops, and efficient functions with no recursion guaranteed to terminate within a bounded execution time in order to support cooperative tasking [32]. To further clarify, we assume that loops are either unrolled or contained entirely inside a non-preemptive basic block. As a result, the real-time task code represented via series-parallel graphs can be efficiently implemented by most structured programming languages such as C. As such, any preemption placement algorithm may be integrated with preemption threshold scheduling [6] [7] [18] [24].

V. PREEMPTION PLACEMENT OBJECTIVE Using the specified series-parallel graph structure, the objective of any preemption placement algorithm is to select a single set of effective preemption points ρ i that minimizes the WCET+CRPD of each task whose real-time conditional code is given by graph G i , subject to the constraint that all non-preemptive regions must be less than or equal to the maximum allowable non-preemptive region parameter Q i . This objective is formally stated as: Preemption Placement Objective: Given a real-time conditional flow graph G i , an interdependent CRPD cost function ξ i (δ x i , δ y i ) and WCET b j i for each basic block, find a set of Effective Preemption Points (EPPs) ρ i ⊆ E that minimizes the cost function Φ i (G i , ρ i ). The cost function Φ i (G i , ρ i ) quantifies the maximum WCET + CRPD for any program path from the start to completion of a task τ i 's job, given the EPP ρ i . Informally, Φ i (G i , ρ i ) sums up the values of ξ i for all pairs of preemption points along a path of a program and adds these preemption costs to the execution time of that path, returning the maximum. Previous work [1]- [3] describes how to compute the term ξ i . The preemption placement problem chooses the ρ i that minimizes Φ under the constraints that the set of EPPs ρ i is subject to the constraint that the sum of the WCET + CRPD along any path between two adjacent preemption points is bounded by Q i . The formal definition depends upon the underlying graph structure and is not explicitly given here. However, a formal definition of Φ is not needed for understanding our proposed algorithm. Thus, we will assume that a preemption placement algorithm exists that minimizes Φ for the underlying CFG structure (e.g., see [6] [7] [18] [24] for more details on these algorithms). In this paper, we only require the property that any preemption placement algorithm the resulting WCET + CRPD returned be exact and monotonically non-decreasing in Q i . This property is easily satisfied by all known preemption placement algorithms [6] [7] [18] [24].

div.head: VI. PPP/PTS SCHEDULABILITY ANALYSIS
div.p: In this section, the analysis presented for prior work in the areas of FP [25] limited preemption scheduling, and PTS [8], [22] scheduling summarizes the computation of the maximum non-preemptive region parameter Q i supporting preemption point placement algorithms.

The goal of schedulability analysis is to determine whether a taskset is schedulable under the worst case task activation pattern. The worst case activation pattern for task τ i , results in the maximum response time. Earlier work proved the maximum response time can occur anywhere within the leveli active period [26]. For a given task τ i , the level-i active period begins with the simultaneous release of jobs belonging to task τ i and all higher priority tasks hp(i) known as the critical instant. This interval is completed when all jobs released at the critical instant have completed [26]:
div.formula: Definition 1. Level-i Active Period: The level-i active period L i is an interval [t 1 , t 2 )
div.p: where the pending workload is positive for all t ∈ (t 1 , t 2 ) and zero at t 1 and t 2 .

div.head: A. Review of Limited Preemption FP Scheduling
div.p: In this section, the schedulability analysis for limited preemption FP scheduling using fixed preemption points is reviewed. For limited preemption FP scheduling, the set of higher priority tasks is represented by:
div.formula: hp(i) = {k | π k > π i }(2)
div.p: where π j represents the assigned nominal priority for task τ j .

To facilitate the schedulability analysis for FP limited preemption scheduling, the request bound function RBF (t) is used to examine the maximum cumulative execution requests in an interval of length t generated by jobs of τ i [27]:
div.formula: RBF i (t) = t T i (C N P i + γ i )(3)
div.p: where γ i denotes the preemption cost due to preemption by higher priority tasks hp(i) during execution of task τ i .
Starting with the critical instant, the cumulative execution request in an interval t for task τ i and all higher priority FP tasks is given by [7]:
div.formula: W LP S i (t) = j∈i∪hp(i) RBF j (t)(4)
div.p: One way to look at this limited preemption FP schedulability constraint is to characterize the amount of blocking tolerance β LP S i that a task τ i can withstand while meeting its deadlines [7]:
div.formula: β LP S i = L i T i -1 min k=0 max t∈[kTi,kTi+Di) t -W LP S i (t)(5)
div.p: (See Equation 30in Section VII for a formal definition of L i ). Characterized by the non-preemptive regions inherent to limited preemption scheduling, the analysis must take into account the longest NP region in the lower priority tasks. The maximum NP region q max i in task τ i must satisfy [7]:
div.formula: q max i ≤ Q i = min h∈hp(i) β LP S h(6)
div.p: We can also characterize the blocking factor B LP S i each task τ i experiences which is given by [7]:
div.formula: B LP S i = max l∈lp(i) {q max l }(7)
div.p: where q max l is the maximum non-preemptive region for task τ l and the set of lower priority tasks lp(i) is given by:
div.formula: lp(i) = {l | π l < π i }(8)

div.head: B. Review of Preemption Threshold Scheduling
div.p: In this section, the schedulability analysis for FP preemption threshold scheduling is reviewed. For PTS scheduling, the set of higher priority tasks is represented by two different conditions: 1) when a job completes and the scheduler must select the next task job to execute, and 2) when a higher priority task preempts an existing task during its execution. The first condition is given by Equation 2. The second condition is given by [28]:
div.formula: ht(i) = {k | π k > θ i }(9)
div.p: In PTS, the tasks that may preempt task τ i have a nominal priority π k exceeding the computed preemption threshold θ i .

The mapping of nominal task priorities π k for each task in a task set is denoted by Π. The mapping of preemption threshold priorities θ i for each task in a task set is denoted by Θ. Higher priority tasks that can block task τ i are those that cannot preempt τ i due to preemption threshold assignments is given by [28]:
div.formula: b h (i) = hp(i) \ ht(i)(10)
div.p: The set of lower priority tasks that may block task τ i in cases where they are activated just before task τ i is given by [28]:
div.formula: b l (i) = lp(i) \ lt(i)(11)
div.p: where the set of lower priority tasks task τ i can preempt is:
div.formula: lt(i) = {l | θ l < π i }(12)
div.p: To facilitate the schedulability analysis for PTS scheduling, the request bound function [27] RBF (t) is also used to examine the maximum cumulative execution request in an interval of length t generated by jobs of τ i per Equation 3.

Starting with the critical instant, the cumulative execution request in an interval t for task τ i and all higher priority ht(i), higher priority blocking b h (i) and lower priority blocking b l (i) FPTS tasks is given by [22], [28]:
div.formula: W P T S i (t) = B P T S i + j∈hep(i) RBF j (t)(13)
div.p: where B P T S i represents the blocking factor task τ i experiences per Equation 16 below and hep(i) is given by [28]:
div.formula: hep(i) = ht(i) ∪ b h (i) ∪ i(14)
div.p: Like FP scheduling, we can look at this limited preemption PTS schedulability constraint by characterizing the amount of blocking tolerance β P T S i that a task τ i can withstand while meeting its deadlines [7]:
div.formula: β P T S i = L i T i -1 min k=0 max t∈[kTi,kTi+Di) t -W P T S i (t)(15)
div.p: where the level-i active period L i is computed in Equation 30.
We can also characterize the blocking factor B P T S i each task τ i experiences which is given by [22], [28]:
div.formula: B P T S i = max b∈b l (i) {C b } = max b∈b l (i) {C N P b + γ b }(16)

div.head: C. Integrated Limited Preemption Threshold Scheduling
div.p: In this section, the schedulabilty analysis for limited preemption scheduling integrated with preemption threshold scheduling is presented. The blocking tolerance is [7]:
div.formula: β LP P T S i = L i T i -1 min k=0 max t∈[kTi,kTi+Di) t -W P T S i (t)(17)
div.p: where the level-i active period L i is computed in Equation 33.
We can also characterize the blocking factor B m i each task τ i experiences which is given by:
div.formula: B m i = max{B LP S i , B P T S i }(18)
div.p: Substituting Equations 7 and 16 into Equation 18, we have:
div.formula: B m i = max( max l∈lp(i) {q max l }, max b∈b l (i) {C N P b + γ b })(19)

div.formula: q max i ≤ Q i = min h∈hp(i) β LP P T S h(20)

div.head: D. Limited Preemption Threshold Scheduling Analysis
div.p: In this section, we integrate the schedulability analysis of PTS and limited preemption FP scheduling. We start by observing that since the lowest priority task τ l is subjected to no blocking, by convention we have B LP S l = 0. We can use the schedulability analysis derived for floating nonpreemptive regions [29] to establish task set schedulability in each case:
div.formula: ∀k ∈ [0, L i T i -1), ∃ t ∈ [kT i , kT i +D i ), W LP S i (t)+B m i ≤ t(21)
div.p: With suitable expressions for β x i introduced, we can express the task set limited preemption schedulability constraint for FP, and PTS scheduling as summarized in Theorem 1 [7]. Theorem 1. A task set τ is schedulable with limited preemption (floating preemption point) scheduling if and only
div.formula: if, ∀i | 1 ≤ i ≤ n, B LP S i ≤ β LP S i (22)
div.p: We can restate the taskset schedulability constraint in terms of the maximum non-preemptive region parameter Q i via Theorem 2 [7].
Theorem 2. A task set τ is schedulable with limited preemption (floating preemption point) scheduling if and only
div.formula: if, ∀i | 1 < i ≤ n, q max i ≤ Q i (23)
div.p: For preemption threshold scheduling, the taskset schedulability constraint can be expressed in terms of Equation 22via Theorem 3 [22], [28].
div.formula: Theorem 3. A task set τ is schedulable with preemption threshold scheduling if, ∀i | 1 < i ≤ n, C b ≤ β P T S i ∀ b ∈ b l (i)(24)
div.p: In summary, to ensure taskset schedulability in preemption threshold scheduling, a task may execute non-preemptively as long as its worst case execution time C b is bounded by β P T S h for all higher priority tasks h ∈ hp(i).

div.head: VII. RESPONSE TIME ANALYSIS
div.p: In this section, response time analysis for prior work in the areas of FP limited preemption scheduling [25] and PTS [8], [22] is presented, summarizing the computation of the worst case response time of tasks under each scheduling paradigm. Response time analysis is used in the PTS optimal threshold assignment algorithm presented in Section VIII and in checking taskset schedulability as a means of comparing the scheduling methods in our evaluation. In each subsection, we begin by computing the time period associated with the worst-case task activation pattern, known as the leveli active period, for each task τ i in the task set τ . For limited preemption FP threshold scheduling, the worst case activation pattern occurs when all higher priority tasks are activated coincident with the activation of task τ i with the activation of the blocking task with the largest execution cost just prior to that of task τ i . We subsequently compute the worst case starting and finishing times in accordance with the scheduling algorithm. Finally, the worst case response time is the maximum difference between the finish time F i,k any of the k jobs in the level-i active period and the start time of the k th job. In the following subsections, we present the response time analysis for fixed priority limited preemption and preemption threshold scheduling. These results will be subsequently utilized in our algorithm integrating preemption placement with optimal threshold assignment.

div.head: A. Limited Preemption FP Scheduling with PPP
div.p: Under FP scheduling, a set of tasks is schedulable if and only if the worst-case response time R i of every task τ i in the task set is bounded by its deadline D i . The computation of the worst-case response time R i is done within an interval known as the level-i active period or level-i busy interval. For limited preemption FP scheduling, the length of the level-i active period is bounded by [25]:
div.formula: L i = j∈hep(i) E j (L i ) • Φ j (G j , ρ j ) + max l∈lp(i) Q l (25
div.p: where the max l∈lp(j) Q l represents the worst case blocking experienced by task τ i inherent to limited preemption scheduling and the term E j (t) is given by [25]:
div.formula: E j (t) = t/T j(26)
div.p: The start time S i,k of the k + 1 th job of task τ i in the level-i busy internal is given by [25]:
div.formula: S i,k = k•Φ i (G i , ρ i )+ max l∈lp(i) Q l + j∈hp(i) E j (S i,k )•Φ j (G j , ρ j )(27)
div.p: The start time S i,k accounts for the k previous invocations of task τ i with worst-case blocking included plus the number of invocations of higher priority tasks within the given start time period. The finish time F i,k of the k + 1 th job of task τ i in the level-i busy internal is given by [25]:
div.formula: F i,k = S i,k + Φ i (G i , ρ i ) + j∈hp(i) (E j (F i,k ) -E j (S i,k )) • Φ j (G j , ρ j )(28)
div.p: The finish time F i,k adds the invocation of task τ i to the computed start time S i,k plus the number of invocations of higher priority tasks between the start time and finish time interval. The worst case response time R i of task τ i in the level-i busy internal is given by [25]:
div.formula: R i = max k≤Ei(Li) (F i,k -kT i )(29)

div.head: B. Limited Preemption FP Threshold Scheduling with PPP
div.p: For limited preemption FP threshold scheduling, the length of the level-i active period is bounded by [8], [22]:
div.formula: L i = j∈hep(i) E j (L i ) • Φ j (G j , ρ j ) + max max l∈lt(i) Q l , max b∈b l (i) Φ b (G b , ρ b ) (30)
div.p: where b l (i) represents the set of tasks that may block task τ i which for limited preemption threshold scheduling is given by Equation 11and where lt(i) is given by Equation 12. For limited preemption threshold scheduling, the start time S i,k of the k + 1 th job of task τ i is given by [8], [22]:
div.formula: S i,k = k • Φ i (G i , ρ i ) + j∈hp(i) E j (S i,k ) • Φ j (G j , ρ j ) + max max l∈lt(i) Q l , max b∈b l (i) Φ b (G b , ρ b ) (31)
div.p: The start time S i,k accounts for the k previous invocations of task τ i with worst-case blocking included plus the number of invocations of higher priority tasks within the given start time period. The finish time F i,k of the k th job of task τ i is given by [8], [22]:
div.formula: F i,k = S i,k + Φ i (G i , ρ i ) + j∈ht(i) (E j (F i,k ) -E j (S i,k )) • Φ j (G j , ρ j )(32)
div.p: The finish time F i,k adds the invocation of task τ i to the computed start time S i,k plus the number of invocations of higher priority tasks between the start time and finish time interval. The worst case response time R i of task τ i is given by Equation 29.

div.head: VIII. INTEGRATED PREEMPTION PLACEMENT AND THRESHOLD ASSIGNMENT ALGORITHM
div.p: In this section, we present the integration of limited preemption FP scheduling with FP preemption threshold scheduling. The integration consists of an iterative algorithm combining PPP with OTA.

div.head: A. High-Level Overview
div.p: Limited preemption scheduling and preemption threshold scheduling are complimentary in that they use the execution time slack inherent in the task set τ to permit tasks to execute non-preemptively. Limited preemption scheduling accomplishes this via a task parameter Q i specifying task τ i 's maximum non-preemptive execution time within which the task set τ remains schedulable. In essence, limited preemption scheduling divides each task τ i into a sequence of nonpreemptive execution regions bounded by Q i . In preemption threshold scheduling, preemption thresholds are adjusted for circumstances where the execution slack of task τ i can completely subsume the execution time of task τ b while still meeting its deadline, the preemption threshold of task τ b is adjusted upwards to prevent it from being preempted by task τ i . Each method attempts to introduce non-preemptive execution into a task set τ commensurate with its real-time execution characteristics. One of the primary differences in these two methods is the level of granularity at which the non-preemptive regions are established. Limited preemption scheduling divides each task into non-preemptive regions or chunks whereas preemption threshold scheduling permits non-preemptive execution at the task level.

div.head: B. Preemption Placement and OTA Integration
div.p: In this section, we present an algorithm that integrates preemption placement with optimal threshold assignment as summarized in Algorithm 1. We use a slightly modified version of Equation 30 by substituting the term C b for the term Φ b to compute an upper bound on the level-i active period term L i given by:
div.formula: L i = j∈hep(i) E j (L i )•Φ j (G j , ρ j ) + max max l∈lt(i) Q l , max b∈b l (i) C b (33)
div.p: We also use a slightly modified version of Equation 17by substituting for the term W P T S i using Equation 13 and setting the term B P T S i = 0 to compute the task τ i blocking tolerance β i term as given by:
div.formula: β i = L i T i -1 min k=0 {β k i }(34)

div.p: Equation 34 computes the minimum task τ i blocking tolerance over all released jobs in the level-i active period L i . Equation 35 computes the maximum blocking tolerance for job k of task τ i . The algorithm begins by initializing the variables θ i , Q i , C i , and ρ i . We start with setting each task's preemption threshold θ i to the highest priority with the default state resulting in each task executing non-preemptively (line 6). Consistent with the non-preemptive execution defaults, we initialize the variables Q i and C i to be the task nonpreemptive execution time C N P i (lines 7, 8). Lastly we initialize the task preemption solution ρ i to be the empty set (line 9). At a high level, we process each task in the task set, computing the level-i active period L i and the blocking tolerance β i (lines 12, 13). If the blocking tolerance is less than zero, we return the task as unschedulable (lines [14][15][16]. Next we analyze the potential blocking introduced by all lower priority tasks (line 17). If either the maximum non-preemptive region parameter Q l or the WCET+CRPD variable C l exceeds the blocking tolerance of task τ i (line 18), then we set the maximum preemption threshold θ l such that task τ l cannot block task τ i (line 19). We also constrain the maximum non-preemptive region Q l of task τ l to the blocking tolerance β i of task τ i (line 20). With the modified maximum non-preemptive region parameter Q l , we perform preemption point placement using Q l and Θ with the set hep(i) as the preempting tasks (lines 21,22). Following preemption placement, we update the WCET+CRPD variable C l with the computed preemption placement costs (line 23). Once each task has been considered along with analyzing the potential blocking introduced by lower priority tasks, we return schedulable (line 27). A proof of correctness and discussion of our integrated preemption placement and maximum threshold assignment is given next.

div.head: C. Integrated PPP/OTA Algorithm Proof of Correctness
div.p: In this section, we prove the correctness of the integrated preemption placement and maximum preemption threshold assignment algorithm as detailed in Algorithm 1.

Theorem 4. Given a task set τ , preemption threshold assignment Θ, and preemption placement assignment for each task ρ i , the task set τ is schedulable with limitedpreemption/preemption-threshold assignment if and only if
div.formula: ∀i | 1 ≤ i ≤ n, (Q l ≤ β i ) ∧ (C b ≤ β i ) ∀ l ∈ lp(i) ∀ b ∈ b l (i) (36)
div.p: Proof: We first prove that scheduability implies Equation 36. Using the result of Theorem 1, we have:
div.formula: B LP P T S i ≤ β LP P T S i ∀i | 1 ≤ i ≤ n (37) max(B LP S i , B P T S i ) ≤ min(β LP S i , β P T S i )(38)
div.p: Note that the value Q l is determined from the preemption placement assignment ρ l , and the set b l (i) is determined by the given preemption-threshold assignment Θ. Substituting Equations 7 and 16 for B LP S i and B P T S i respectively, and using the schedulability constraint result in Equation 36 of Theorem 4 we have:
div.formula: max[ max l∈lp(i) {Q l }, max b∈b l (i) {C b }] ≤ β P T S i (39)
div.p: Substituting Equation 16for C b , we have:

div.formula: max l∈lp(i) {Q l } ≤ β P T S i → Q l ≤ β P T S i ∀l | 1 ∈ lp(i) (41) max b∈b l (i) {C N P b +γ b ) ≤ β P T S i → C N P b +γ b ≤ β P T S i ∀b|b ∈ b l (i) (42)
div.p: Thus proving the integrated schedulability constraint. The sufficiency of Equation 36 can be shown by just reversing the argument (due to the use of exact response-time analysis for sporadic tasks).
We use the schedulability constraint to prove the correctness of Algorithm 1.
Theorem 5. Given a task system τ , after the i'th iteration of the for loop in lines 11-26 (for 1 ≤ i ≤ n), the following statements are true (if "unschedulable" is not returned"):

1) Tasks τ 1 , . . . , τ i are schedulable using the Θ and ρ i assignments computed. 2) For all tasks τ l ∈ lp(i) any preemption threshold assignment with θ l > θ l or preemption placement assignment with Q l > Q l would make {τ 1 , . . . , τ i } unschedulable.
Furthermore, if "unschedulable" is returned by the i'th iteration, then there does not exist a valid assignment of Θ and ρ l for lower-priority tasks to make {τ 1 , . . . , τ i } schedulable.

Proof Sketch: The proof is by induction on i. Base Case: We start with the highest priority task τ 1 . Being the highest priority task, τ 1 executes completely nonpreemptively and its schedulability can be evaluated using the expression C N P 1 ≤ D 1 or β 1 ≥ 0. If the condition β 1 ≤ 0 is true, we return unschedulable (lines 16-18); note, it is unschedulable by any algorithm in this case. Otherwise, β 1 has the computed execution slack or blocking tolerance and for each τ l ∈ lp(1), task τ l can either execute nonpreemptively with θ 1 = π 1 or must be preempted with maximum non-preemptive region Q l = β 1 to maintain τ 1 's schedulability. This implies Statements 1 and 2 hold for the base case. Inductive Step: Assume that Statements 1 and 2 of the theorem hold for iterations 1 through i -1 (Induction Hypothesis Assumption). Now consider the i'th iteration. If β i < 0, the the i'th iteration returns "unschedulable", and task τ i cannot tolerate any blocking given its CRPD overhead (which is minimal by Statement 2 of the induction hypothesis and the optimality/monotonicity of preemption placement). Otherwise, if β i ≥ 0, then β i expresses the maximum non-preemptive region size for any lower-priority task τ l ∈ lp(i). If C l ≤ β i and θ l > π i , then the task τ l can execute non-preemptively and maintain the schedulability of {τ 1 , . . . , τ i }; otherwise, τ l must execute preemptively and it's non-preemptive region is set to the maximum blocking tolerance of τ i or any higher-priority task (line 20). It can easily be verified by setting θ l and Q l according to the assignments in lines 19 and 20 imply the schedulability of {τ 1 , . . . , τ i } (by Theorem 4). In all cases, Statements 1 and 2 continue to hold at the end of the i'th iteration.
Theorem 5 implies that if a schedulable assignment of Θ and ρ exists, then Algorithm 1 is guaranteed to find it (i.e., Algorithm 1 is optimal).

div.head: IX. EVALUATION
div.p: Our integrated PPP/OTA algorithm will be evaluated using breakdown utilization cost metric as a function of cache block reload times.

div.head: A. Task Set Generation
div.p: Our study will utilize synthetically generated task sets of linear CFGs along with task execution parameters for comparing our linear PPP algorithm [18] against our integrated PPP/OTA algorithm. Each experiment generates 1000 different task sets. Target task utilization is swept in accordance with the breakdown utilization algorithm [18]. The number of tasks is randomly selected using a uniform distribution in the interval [8,15]. The number of basic blocks in each task is randomly selected using a uniform distribution in the interval [200,400]. The number of instructions in each basic block is randomly selected using a uniform distribution in the interval [10,100]. The WCET of each basic block is randomly selected using a gaussian distribution with µ = 0 and σ = 5. The absolute value of all generated WCET values are used. Our system employs separate instruction and data direct mapped caches containing N C cache blocks uniformly selected from the set {1024, 2048, 4096} with a total cache utilization U C = 4. The cache block size s is randomly generated using a uniformly selected from the set {8, 16, 32, 64, 128} bytes. The total cache memory size is given by the expression N C • s. The total number of task set cache blocks is given by N C • U C . Individual task cache utilization U C i is generated via the UUniFast algorithm [33] where
div.formula: n i=1 U C i = U C .
div.p: Tasks occupy contiguous memory ordered from highest priority to lowest priority. Individual instructions are determined from the generated memory layout. Individual data accesses are generated via a two pronged approach. Within each basic block, a median RAM memory location M A is generated using a uniform distribution over the RAM memory space. The RAM memory accessed by each instruction is generated using a gaussian distribution with µ = M A and σ = 512 bytes. Reused cached task data accesses have a targeted overlap of 40% with its generated data accesses. Individual task utilization are generated via the UUniFast algorithm [33]. Task periods T i are computed using each task's WCET and task utilization. Task deadlines D i are uniformly sampled in the interval [C N P i + (T i -C N P i )/3, T i /2]. Nominal task priorities Π are assigned in descending order per a Deadline Monotonic policy. The cache block reload time (BRT) parameter is swept from 1 ns to 640 ns per MIPS processor family performance.
1) Availability: The research community may reproduce and leverage our work via the developed programs and analyzed data that will be archived on GitHub.

2) Results: The results are presented as an illustration of the potential benefit of our integrated PPP/OTA algorithm combining limited preemption scheduling with preemption threshold scheduling, in comparison to existing methods.

div.head: B. System Utilization Schedulability
div.p: In this section, we study the performance of limited preemption scheduling using preemption placement only, FPVS, and optimal threshold assignment as baselines, as compared to preemption placement integrated with preemption threshold scheduling via optimal threshold assignment. We perform an average breakdown utilization comparison between the various approaches for 1000 schedulable task sets. The breakdown utilization of a taskset τ is defined as the minimum system utilization U where the taskset becomes unschedulable. By comparing these methods we illustrate the superiority of the integrated preemption placement/preemption threshold scheduling algorithm versus limited preemption scheduling via preemption placement only. Figure 2 illustrates the breakdown utilization comparison. The limited preemption scheduling via preemption placement is denoted as LEPP, the integrated preemption placement/preemption threshold scheduling method is denoted as LEPPOTA, the fixed priority varying threshold scheduling is denoted as FPVS, and the optimal preemption threshold scheduling is denoted as OTA. We chose to omit comparison to existing independent CRPD methods as Bril et al. demonstrated OTA [22] and FPVS [23] to dominate them. For large block reload times, the integrated preemption placement/preemption threshold scheduling algorithm dominates the preemption placement only, FPVS, and OTA algorithms. FPVS is an improvement over OTA due to maximizing non-preemptive execution per taskset execution slack. However, it is encumbered by the use of a task centric CRPD cost model as compared to the interdependent, location aware CRPD cost models used in preemption placement. The ability of the integrated approach to adjust the preemption thresholds to permit tasks to execute non-preemptively where possible has further benefits in reduced preemption placement costs. As expected, all methods converge as the block reload time approaches zero.

div.head: X. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, we presented an algorithm that integrates limited preemption scheduling via preemption placement with preemption threshold scheduling via optimal preemption threshold assignment. Our experiments demonstrated the increased schedulability over existing preemption placement and optimal threshold assignment algorithms. Using the ability of the optimal threshold assignment to allow tasks to execute non-preemptively where feasible, a significant reduction in preemption cost was achieved when combined with preemption placement, resulting from a reduced subset of higher priority tasks for some tasks in a real-time taskset. The improvements were measured using a large number of synthetically generated task sets, achieving up to a 30% increase in breakdown utilization as compared to a standalone preemption placement algorithm. In future work, we plan to evaluate the effect of unique preemption thresholds for each non-preemptive region similar to FPVS.
